recentItems.description:

--------
In this VladTV full interview, West Baltimore half-brothers Marlow Bates and Timmirror “Tamir” Stanfield share their account of the 1980s street era that helped inspire HBO’s Marlo Stanfield on The Wire. They discuss growing up in the projects, the rise of heroin in Baltimore, Murphy Homes, New York connections, and crossing paths with figures like Little Melvin Williams.

Bates and Stanfield also address their murder convictions, double-life sentences, claims of fabricated evidence, former detective Ed Burns, creator David Simon, and the impact of discredited ballistics expert Joseph Chaperro. The conversation covers Jamie Hector’s portrayal, prison life, losing family while locked up, and their release after nearly four decades.

Now focused on accountability and community, they reflect on the damage drugs caused in Baltimore, their Amazon Prime documentary People Say It’s Nice, and the TV project they say will tell more of their story.

Rainwater sits down with VladTV to reflect on his path from Dallas and Cedar Hill party promoter to managing Mo3 during the rapper’s rise. He opens up about serving time after burglary of habitation charges tied to college dorm break-ins, a jail experience that changed his outlook, and how he met Mo3 shortly after coming home in 2014. Rainwater recalls hearing Mo3’s music through a woman named Crystal, comparing his voice to “the next Kurt Cobain,” then building a close business relationship based on a 50/50 handshake deal with no paperwork. The interview also looks at the DFW rap scene, Oak Cliff, early booking work with dance-era artists, and the long-running tension between Mo3 and Yella Beezy, who Rainwater says were often around each other but never truly close.

In this VladTV interview, Jimmy DiModica recalls entering New York’s after-hours club scene around age 20, dealing blackjack for Alley Boy Persico on East 75th Street and crossing paths with Colombo boss Carmine “The Snake” Persico, aka “The Immortal.” DiModica describes Persico’s upstate Saugerties estate, the fallout from mob cases in the early 1980s, and his move into Staten Island nightlife with Johnny “Moose,” identified as a Gambino Mafia soldier, who DiModica says ordered him to beat people up during chaotic nights at the Ritz Theater on Richmond Terrace.

The conversation covers alleged ties to Johnny DiLeo, the Genovese Jersey faction, Bonanno associates, cocaine-era club violence, illegal after-hours spots, and a reported Staten Island Advance shootout involving Michael Erico. DiModica also explains why he avoided carrying guns inside clubs and how police encounters, gambling rooms, and mob politics shaped daily survival in 1980s La Cosa Nostra circles.

In this VladTV interview, John Franzese Jr. reflects on rebuilding his life through sobriety, marriage, disability income and Section 8 housing before his father reentered the picture after prison. He discusses reluctantly visiting his dad, meeting Henry Hill of *Goodfellas* fame in Los Angeles, and how Hill’s struggle to leave the past behind shaped his own thinking about cooperation and becoming a confidential informant.

Franzese also breaks down the Colombo crime family hierarchy in the mid-2000s, including Carmine “The Snake” Persico and acting street boss Thomas “Tommy Shots” Gioeli, who elevated his father to underboss. As pressure returned through requests to “do favors,” Franzese recalls being pulled toward mob business again, including alleged discussions involving Nicky Bova, before entering the Witness Security Program in 2006. A candid look at addiction, loyalty, organized crime and the cost of walking away.

Tito “TJ” Dominguez sits down with Vlad to reflect on life after serving 14 years in federal prison, including probation, asset seizures, and what he calls “diesel therapy” during prisoner transport. Now 74 and starting over, Dominguez explains how losing cars, homes, money, jewelry, and planes left him broke—but also pushed him toward a legal comeback with his sunscreen and lip balm company, Miami Sun, developed while in solitary confinement.

He also revisits the 1980s cocaine era in Miami, saying the culture wasn’t simply “Just Say No,” but a party-driven world involving wealthy customers, professionals, and escalating violence tied to Colombia. Dominguez discusses attorney Fred Schwartz, rebuilding in San Diego and Texas, plans to take Miami Sun public, and international interest from Dubai. The conversation also touches on Boston George, Johnny Depp’s *Blow*, and the danger of chasing “one more deal.”

In this VladTV interview, Rene “Boxer” Enriquez reflects on the regret, violence, and personal accountability that followed his decades in the California prison system. Enriquez discusses being found guilty in two deaths, the character flaws he still works to control, and why he says he “earned” parole through psychological evaluations and meeting California Penal Code standards—not through a secret federal deal.

The conversation also explores his extensive cooperation with law enforcement, including testimony in 65 trials, and how that became a double-edged sword during parole hearings and gubernatorial reviews. Enriquez details repeated reversals, media scrutiny, comparisons to high-profile privilege narratives like the Diddy case, and a major court battle involving Judge William Ryan at the Clara Shortridge Foltz Criminal Justice Center.

After more than 30 years incarcerated, Enriquez talks about freedom, redemption, aging, and his new uncensored YouTube platform.

--------
Former DEA agent Chris Feistl breaks down the 1995 takedown of the Cali Cartel leadership with Vlad, detailing how investigators tracked Gilberto Rodríguez Orejuela through his assistant “Flaco,” using static surveillance tactics reminiscent of Zero Dark Thirty. Feistl explains why cartel bosses like Miguel Rodríguez Orejuela avoided armed clashes with Colombian police and U.S. agents, and how Colombia’s no-extradition policy shaped arrests after Pablo Escobar’s war with the government.

The interview also covers the July 4 arrest of José Santacruz Londoño at a Bogotá steakhouse, the role of the Colombian National Police, Search Bloc, DEA and CIA, and how insider Jorge Salcedo’s cooperation helped expose Miguel Rodríguez’s location in Cali. From surveillance detection to compromised law enforcement units, this segment offers a grounded look at one of the most important drug trafficking investigations in Colombia’s history.
